extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor, literature, and philosophy (and theatre practitioners interested in comic theory)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical/critical analysis of the mechanisms that produce the comic, with theatrical and literary examples — centering on a core law (mechanical rigidity superposed on the living) and three main directions of development (rigidity/fashion, body vs soul, person→thing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical encrusted on the living (central law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic arises when something mechanical (rigidity, automatism, a ready-made form) is superposed upon what is living and supple — when life suggests a machine working inside the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the fundamental principle from which many comic effects follow. Examples and consequences appear across gestures, costume, society, and language; treat this as the primary diagnostic: ask whether the situation suggests a mechanism or machine behind human behaviour. Analysis and reflection can render fleeting mechanical glimpses permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS ARE LAUGHABLE IN PROPORTION AS THEY REMIND US OF A MERE MACHINE
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures and movements that make us clearly perceive a person as a jointed puppet—i.e., look mechanically uniform rather than living—produce laughter in proportion to the clarity and subtlety of that suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drawings, acting, or descriptions by how distinctly they allow the audience to see both 'person' and 'mechanism' simultaneously. Good comic art balances clarity of the machine-image with retaining enough life to make the contrast striking. Beware of relied-on textual context: if the laugh comes from the text/situation rather than the gesture itself, it is not intrinsic to the gesture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition/automatism as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeated, always-the-same movement, word, or scene — expected and automatic — turns life into automatism and provokes laughter (e.g., a speaker who repeats the same head or arm movement at regular intervals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify periodic repetition (words, scenes, gestures). On stage and in text, repetition should suggest mechanical regularity. Overuse without variation may flatten the effect; controlled repetition that reveals expected automatism works best. Repetition is also the basis of many dramatic contrivances (periodic repetition of a word/scene, inversion, geometric development of farce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation increases comic effect by revealing automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: A gesture that is not laughable in one person becomes laughable when imitated by another because imitation exposes its mechanical uniformity—showing that the original ceased to be fully alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance or parody, imitation should emphasize the uniformity/mechanism behind a gesture. Parody can deflect gestures toward a mechanical occupation (sawing wood, tugging a rope) to make them appear intentionally mechanical and increase laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and absolute uniformity (marionette effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several people move/dance/gesticulate in the same way simultaneously, the uniformity suggests marionettes or invisible threads joining them, magnifying the comic by making living bodies seem stiff and automaton-like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for choruses or ensemble pieces that synchronize movement; the stronger and more absolute the uniformity, the more the audience perceives puppetry. Effective in choreography and stage business; avoid accidental variation that breaks the illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise and fashion: rigid covering vs living suppleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothing, fashion, or any adopted covering may become laughable when perceived as incongruous with the living body — especially when continuity breaks and the costume is mentally isolated from the person (e.g., anachronistic dress, top hat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often isolates the form (dress, fashion) from its usual assimilation to the person. A sudden dissolution of custom makes the latent comic visible. Evaluate whether the costume calls attention to itself and thus creates an image of disguise or masquerade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of artificiality (skin/colour as 'painted')
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination may treat inherent bodily features (a black face, a red nose) as if they were painted or applied disguises; this perception of artificial coating produces comic effects by invoking masquerade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an observation about imaginative perception rather than an endorsement. Historically used to explain comic reactions to colouration and abrupt visual surprise. Exercise cultural and ethical caution: the passage discusses racialized examples in psychological explanation, not prescribing their use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony and formula: form supplants matter (latent comic in social ritual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonies and formalities become comic when attention is fixed on the form (the formula) rather than the underlying serious matter — making participants appear as puppets obeying a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social scenes by whether ritualized behaviour is foregrounded and thereby exposed as automatism (e.g., prize-distribution, court sittings). Comedy can be produced by isolating ceremonial form from its purpose; examples include officials performing rules even in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional automatism / manner outdoing matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Professions become laughable when manner, outward form, or adherence to rules replaces the substantive ends they are meant to serve (the means become the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify characters or figures whose behaviour is governed by scrupulous observance of form (doctors, lawyers, officials). Comic portrayal often duplicates professional ridiculousness with physical ridiculousness (see 'overtones' criterion). Molière's doctors are cited as paradigmatic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: The body taking precedence over the soul (physical intrusion into moral/intellectual moment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any incident that draws attention to a person's physicality at a moment when the moral/intellectual aspect should dominate is comic (e.g., a speaker sneezing at a pathetic moment; a hero sitting down during tragedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing a comic moment, check whether the material/body interrupts or undermines the intended moral/intellectual register. Tragedy avoids such intrusions; comedy exploits them. Small bodily details (toothache, tight shoes) can be mined for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical defect mirroring intellectual/moral defect (overtone law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical peculiarities (stammering, slowness of speech, stutter) are used to prefigure or complete a representation of intellectual ossification or professional incapacity; comic work often pairs a physical flaw with a corresponding moral or intellectual failing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In staging and characterization, use vocal or physical quirks as 'overtones' that foreshadow the larger comic trait. This duplication strengthens the audience's associative recognition of the ridiculous. Beware of crude or gratuitous disability-mocking—aim for structural, not merely mean-spirited, linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: We laugh when a person gives the impression of being a thing (objectification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic images arise when a person progressively appears to the imagination as an object (ball, dummy, bundle): the gradual solidifying of a vague image into a thing is especially effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include accelerated, rhythmic movement, crescendoing rebounds, exaggeration of solidity and rigidity, and gradual suggestion that the human form becomes a mass or machine. Clowning examples: bodies becoming rubber balls; men turned into wooden dummies. Use graded suggestion to move audience perception from human to thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion/solidification by graded hints
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective method for creating the illusion of mechanisation or objectification is gradual suggestion: start from perceivable reality and make perceptions more indefinite, then let them solidify into the intended mechanical/thing-image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a compositional technique for comedy: build the hallucination step-by-step (as in hypnotic suggestion or visual solidification at sleep onset). In performance, rhythm, escalation, and repetition can accomplish this. Instant or blunt imposition of the image may be less effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic/linguistic devices that lull imagination toward objectification
rubrics_metrics.description: By arranging rhythm, rhyme and assonance, a poet or writer can rock the imagination between like elements and thus prepare it to accept an image of a person as a doll or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In verbal comedy, analyze sound and prosodic patterns for their capacity to lull or regularize perception. Assonance/rhythm can be exploited to create a gentle, see-sawing mental state in which objectifying suggestions land more readily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic vs borrowed comic (drawing vs text/situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic element in a drawing or performance may be intrinsic (in the visual itself) or borrowed from accompanying text/situation; intrinsic comic relies on the image alone to suggest mechanicality or incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a comic piece, distinguish whether laughter is produced by the drawing/gesture itself or by external narrative/satire. For craft, prefer intrinsic devices when the goal is purely visual/physical comedy; use borrowed satire intentionally and not as a crutch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent comic extinguished by continuity/custom; requires rupture to emerge
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things are comic 'de jure' (in principle) but not comic 'de facto' because habit and custom deaden the comic quality; a sudden dissolution of continuity (anachronism, surprise) is required to revive the comic aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a comic effect depends on breaking an accepted continuity (fashion change, anachronism). Use rupture strategically to reveal the latent comic rather than inventing novelty for its own sake. This also cautions against assuming surprise alone equals comedy.
